Expectation1: Be considerate with shared spaces and boundaries
Situation1: My dog becomes vocal in the hallway when people pass near shared doors.
Expectation2: Support individuals or groups in accessing essential services and resources
Situation2: They casually guide a youth, an older adult, or a refugee family toward available social or community services.
Story:
I heard my dog barking again, his sharp voice echoing down the hallway. I rushed out, apologizing to Mrs. Kim, who was carrying groceries past our door. As a neighbor, I know I’m expected to keep the peace, to make sure my dog doesn’t disturb others, especially in our close-knit apartment building. I promised Mrs. Kim I’d work on it, feeling her frustration as she nodded and hurried away.

Minutes later, I spotted Mr. Rahim, the new tenant from Syria, standing uncertainly by the mailboxes. As an advocate, I’m always ready to help—he looked lost, and I knew he needed guidance on how to access the community food pantry. But as I approached, my dog started barking again, louder this time, drawing annoyed glances from behind closed doors. I felt torn—should I rush my dog inside to keep the peace, or stay and help Mr. Rahim navigate these unfamiliar systems? The weight of both roles pressed on me, each demanding something I couldn’t give at the same time. My heart pounded as I stood between my barking dog and Mr. Rahim’s hopeful eyes, unsure which expectation to meet first.
